description: Reader-facing micro-wiki for lightly mentioned historical people, families, clans, factions, institutions, events, places and named historical works through Book VI. The novel provides the trigger and an authoritative external source provides concise historical context.

source_policy.novel_trigger_source: Canonical local chapter corpus under data/source/book1 through data/source/book6
source_policy.rule: Never merge external historical facts into novel evidence.

novel_trigger.context: Why the reference matters at this point

wiki.summary: Two or three concise lines of salient historical context.

novel_trigger.context: Historical commander whose actions at Sekigahara are described in the opening scene.

wiki.summary: Daimyo who commanded a major contingent at Sekigahara. His decision to switch allegiance to Tokugawa Ieyasu was a decisive factor in the Eastern Army's victory.

source.title: Kobayakawa Hideaki Route
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Principal Western Army commander named in the opening description of Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Toyotomi administrator and leading commander of the Western Army at Sekigahara. He opposed Tokugawa Ieyasu and was defeated at the battle that established Tokugawa supremacy.

source.title: Ishida Mitsunari Route
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Major Western Army commander named among the defeated commanders at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Major Toyotomi ally who commanded the largest Western Army contingent at Sekigahara. His forces fought in the main battle against the Tokugawa-led coalition.

source.title: Fukushima Masanori Route — Ukita Hideie’s Encampment
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Western Army commander named among the forces defeated at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Daimyo of Satsuma who commanded the Shimazu contingent at Sekigahara. After the Western Army collapsed, he fought his way through the opposing ranks and returned to Satsuma.

source.title: Ishida Mitsunari Route — Shimazu Yoshihiro’s Encampment
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Western Army commander named among the defeated commanders at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Commander of a Western Army contingent at Sekigahara. After the Western Army was routed, Konishi fled, surrendered, and was executed in Kyoto together with Ishida Mitsunari.

source.title: Kuroda Nagamasa Route — Konishi Yukinaga’s Encampment
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Leader of the victorious Eastern coalition identified in the opening aftermath of Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Leader of the Eastern coalition at Sekigahara and the central figure in the Tokugawa victory. His triumph over the Western coalition established Tokugawa political dominance in Japan.

source.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu Route
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: The battle whose immediate aftermath forms the opening setting of Book I.

wiki.summary: The decisive 1600 battle between the Tokugawa-led coalition and the forces aligned with the Toyotomi cause. The victory shifted the balance of power decisively toward Tokugawa Ieyasu.

source.title: About the Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Victorious coalition at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Modern shorthand for the coalition led by Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara. The Gifu museum notes that these 'Eastern' and 'Western' labels were not actually used at the time of the battle.

source.title: About the Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: Defeated coalition at Sekigahara.

wiki.summary: Modern shorthand for the coalition opposing Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara and associated with the Toyotomi cause. The label is useful for readers, although it was not the period's own terminology.

source.title: About the Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum
source.publisher: Gifu Sekigahara Battlefield Memorial Museum / Gifu Prefecture

novel_trigger.context: The novel states that the Hon'iden and Shimmen families trace their lineage to the Akamatsu house.

wiki.summary: A major samurai house of Harima that rose to prominence as shugo-daimyo during the Muromachi period. The Hyogo Prefectural Museum of History documents the clan's long political and military presence in western Harima.

novel_trigger.context: Takuan recalls the legend of Hiromasa playing the flute at the Suzaku Gate in Kyoto.

wiki.summary: A Heian-period court noble and celebrated gagaku musician (918–980), especially known as a master of wind instruments. The National Theatre of Japan records him as the compiler of the 966 flute notation collection known as Hakuga's flute score.

source.title: The lives of gagaku musicians — Heian period

context_source.title: The Story of Minamoto no Hiromasa and the Demon's Flute

novel_trigger.context: Lord Ikeda explains the Shimmen family's historical connection to the Akamatsu lineage and names Masanori in that genealogy.

wiki.summary: Akamatsu Masanori (1455–1496) was a medieval military lord and shugo who restored the Akamatsu family's position in Harima, Bizen and Mimasaka. He died in 1496, after which the family passed to his adopted heir Yoshimura.

novel_trigger.context: The chapter title and Takuan's discussion invoke Sunzi's Art of War as a framework for strategy and conduct.

wiki.summary: An ancient Chinese military treatise traditionally attributed to Sunzi (Sun Tzu). Its exact composition date is debated, but it is generally associated with the late Warring States / early classical military tradition.

novel_trigger.context: The opening of Book II uses Nobunaga's career and death to frame Kyoto's recent political past.

wiki.summary: Japanese military leader (1534–1582) whose campaigns transformed the late Sengoku political order. The authority source fixes identity and dates; the novel's interpretation remains literary context.

novel_trigger.context: Book II's opening chronology names Hideyoshi as Nobunaga's successor and as the predecessor to Tokugawa supremacy.

wiki.summary: Japanese ruler (1536–1598) who held the office of kanpaku. The institutional authority record also preserves Hashiba Hideyoshi among his variant names.

novel_trigger.context: The political introduction states that Ieyasu transferred the shogunal title to his third son Hidetada.

wiki.summary: Second Tokugawa shogun (1579–1632), son of Tokugawa Ieyasu. This historical identification does not validate the novel's broader political narration.

novel_trigger.context: Book II names Hideyori at Osaka Castle while explaining the unsettled Tokugawa–Toyotomi balance.

wiki.summary: Son and heir of Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1593–1615), associated with Osaka Castle and the final Toyotomi resistance. Only this general identity is supplied as context.

novel_trigger.context: Seijūrō and his companions discuss attending the popular Okuni performance in Kyoto.

wiki.summary: At the start of the seventeenth century, a woman calling herself an Izumo shrine maiden, Okuni, made kabuki-odori highly popular in Kyoto; the form used song, dance and the fashions of kabukimono.

source.title: The Beginning — History of Kabuki
source.publisher: National Theatre of Japan / Japan Arts Council

novel_trigger.context: Travelers describe the retired Yagyū master at Koyagyū before he later enters the narrative physically.

wiki.summary: Nara City's historical material identifies Yagyū Munetoshi (Sekishūsai, 1527–1606) as a leading Yagyū figure and links his tradition with Kamiizumi Nobutsuna. The novel's meetings and dialogue are not treated as documentary history.

novel_trigger.context: Travelers identify Munenori as Sekishūsai's heir and report that he is away in Edo; this remains a mention, not physical presence.

wiki.summary: Nara City's guide identifies Munenori as Sekishūsai's fifth son, a servant of Tokugawa Ieyasu and sword instructor to the second and third shoguns; he later became the first Yagyū daimyo.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi visits the Hōzōin establishment and confronts its spear tradition.

wiki.summary: A Japanese spear tradition whose official lineage identifies the monk Hōzōin Kakuzenbō Hōin In'ei as founder. The historical school does not authenticate the novel's individual bouts.

novel_trigger.context: Book II names the master associated with In'ei and Yagyū Muneyoshi; the translation's Kōizumi is normalized cautiously to the historically documented Kamiizumi tradition.

wiki.summary: Sword master Kamiizumi Nobutsuna, also styled Ise-no-kami, is linked in Nara City's Yagyū historical material with Sekishūsai. The novel's translated name and anecdotes remain literary evidence.

novel_trigger.context: Matahachi works at the large construction site and later hides in Fushimi.

wiki.summary: Kyoto City's history describes Fushimi as a road-and-water transport hub shaped by Hideyoshi's castle construction and port development. This supports the broad setting, not the exact worksite.

novel_trigger.context: Seijūrō explicitly identifies the previously unnamed young swordsman; this does not identify the earlier dead certificate bearer.

wiki.summary: The National Diet Library maintains a personal-name authority for Sasaki Kojirō as a swordsman and records 1612 as his death year. The novel's biography and encounters remain literary evidence.

novel_trigger.context: The Yoshioka party stays near the shrine and Akemi reaches the Sumiyoshi shore.

wiki.summary: The shrine's official chronology supports its long historical presence at Sumiyoshi while noting scholarly debate around its traditional foundation date. It does not authenticate the novel's inn or shoreline scenes.

novel_trigger.context: The chapter invokes Bokuden while framing sword traditions known to Musashi.

wiki.summary: Kashima City's cultural-property material identifies Bokuden as a historical swordsman born in 1489 and describes traditions associated with his training. The novel's anecdotes remain narrative context.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi approaches Naikū, purifies himself in the Isuzu River and leaves his swords before climbing Eagle Mountain.

wiki.summary: Official Jingū material identifies Naikū and the Uji Bridge over the Isuzugawa at its entrance. This supports the general geography without fixing narrative scene coordinates.

novel_trigger.context: Ujitomi entrusts Otsū with painted scrolls for delivery to Mitsuhiro in Kyoto.

wiki.summary: Institutional catalogues identify Karasumaru Mitsuhiro (1579–1638) as a court noble and writer. His role and residence in the novel are not treated as documentary biography.

context_source.title: Tōkōki cultural-property record
context_source.publisher: Agency for Cultural Affairs / Cultural Heritage Online

novel_trigger.context: The Yoshioka school posts the Rendaiji duel announcement at the bridge.

wiki.summary: Kyoto City's official chronology records construction of the Great Gojō Bridge in 1589. This supports the bridge's period existence, not the exact narrative scene point.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi meets Kōetsu and Myōshū at a tea picnic; the invitation to Hon'ami Lane has not yet become a stay.

wiki.summary: Kyoto National Museum describes Kōetsu (1558–1637) as a calligrapher and maker in lacquer and ceramics from the Hon'ami sword-polishing and appraisal family. His meetings with Musashi remain literary scenes.

source.title: Rinpa: The Aesthetics of the Capital

novel_trigger.context: Musashi and Denshichirō formally establish their duel at Rengeōin.

wiki.summary: The temple's official history identifies Rengeōin with Sanjūsangendō and records its twelfth-century foundation and later rebuilding. It does not authenticate the novel's duel.

novel_trigger.context: Kōetsu names Yoshino while proposing an evening visit to the Ōgiya; Musashi has not yet met her.

wiki.summary: Kyoto's official travel material preserves the cultural memory of the celebrated early-seventeenth-century Yoshino Tayū and associates her with Jōshōji. The novel's setting and encounters may involve literary compression.

source.title: Japanese Musical Instruments Show: Tales from the 1000-year Capital

novel_trigger.context: The Yoshioka men name the spreading pine as the site for their public duel with Musashi.

wiki.summary: Kyoto's official guide identifies an old traffic point and presents the Musashi–Yoshioka episode as a famous legend; the present pine is a later generation. This is not independent proof of the novel's battle.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi is taken to the Mount Hiei temple complex after the Ichijōji battle.

wiki.summary: Enryakuji's official history records Nobunaga's destruction of the complex in 1571 and its gradual reconstruction. That supplies broad period context only; Musashi's stay remains narrative.

novel_trigger.context: The bridge is the intended rendezvous for the eastbound journey; the party has not yet reached Edo.

wiki.summary: The Ōtsu tourism authority identifies Seta no Karahashi as a real and historically prominent bridge. It validates the locality label, not the novel's rendezvous.

source.title: Seta no Karahashi Bridge
source.publisher: Biwako Otsu Travel Guide / Otsu Tourism Association

novel_trigger.context: The eastbound party pauses at the paired waterfalls while Musashi performs austerity.

wiki.summary: Nagiso Tourism Association identifies the two waterfalls near the Tsumago–Magome route with the Musashi–Otsū episode in Yoshikawa's novel. This validates the intended literary location, not historical biography or exact routing.

novel_trigger.context: Karasumaru's letter lets Musashi, Otsū and Jōtarō pass the checkpoint before their separation.

wiki.summary: Kiso Town identifies Fukushima as one of the major Edo-period checkpoints and a transport junction. This supports the broad locality, not the novel's precise passage geometry.

source.title: National Historic Site: Fukushima Barrier Ruins

novel_trigger.context: Reports direct the search for Jōtarō toward Daizō's business in Narai.

wiki.summary: Shiojiri City documents Narai as a Nakasendō post-town settlement along the Narai River. Daizō's premises and the novel's exact movements remain unmapped.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi stops at the hot springs and meets Ishimoda Geki.

wiki.summary: Shimosuwa Town describes the locality as the junction of the Nakasendō and Kōshū routes, a hot-spring post town and a Suwa shrine gateway. The novel's inn and route are not pinpointed.

novel_trigger.context: The separated travelers pass through the temple and Hachiōji streams.

wiki.summary: Hachiōji City's cultural material supports Mount Takao and Yakuōin as a longstanding religious setting. It does not locate the novel's inn, moat or burial mound.

entities.display_name: Early Edo, Nihombashi and the Sumida

novel_trigger.context: Osugi enters the rapidly developing city and reaches Nihombashi.

wiki.summary: Tokyo public authorities document the broad early-Edo development chronology and historical Sumida context. Private homes, ferry points and individual narrative routes remain unresolved.

novel_trigger.context: Yajibei's party travels to Sensōji while a donation plaque supplies only a report about Daizō.

wiki.summary: Sensōji's official history supports the institution's continuity and Sumida origin tradition. The donation plaque and the novel's boat journey remain narrative claims.

novel_trigger.context: A donation record is mentioned while Yajibei's party traces Daizō's reported activity.

wiki.summary: The shrine's official history documents its early-Edo relocations and enshrinement tradition. Daizō's reported donation is not independently authenticated.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi meets Sannosuke in the flood-prone Hōtengahara setting.

wiki.summary: MLIT describes the early-modern eastward diversion of the Tone as a long sequence of works tied to flood control, new fields and transport. This does not identify fictional Hōtengahara.

source.title: Eastward diversion of the Tone River

novel_trigger.context: Iori loses his way while attempting to deliver Musashi's letter to the Yagyū residence.

wiki.summary: Minato City documents Azabu and Iigura as historical place names. The novel's Yagyū residence and Iori's precise route are not geolocated from this correspondence.

source.title: History of place names: Azabu area

novel_trigger.context: Musashi brings the recovering Shinzō within sight of his father's house.

wiki.summary: Shinjuku City's cultural register supports the Akagi shrine tradition in Ushigome while cautioning that parts of the received chronology are estimated. The Hōjō house remains unmapped.

novel_trigger.context: Kojirō's conflict with Yogorō reaches the Isarago cemetery area.

wiki.summary: Minato City's history supports the old Takanawa and Isarago names but does not identify the novel's cemetery or lodging.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi and Iori stop overnight after the typhoon destroys their cabin.

wiki.summary: Official local history supports Tanashi as an old place name; the overnight house is not identifiable.

novel_trigger.context: Iori encounters old battle bones along the route across the plain.

wiki.summary: Tokorozawa City documents the 1333 battlefield. The novel's bones and precise route remain narrative.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi searches donor records and observes the shrine festival musicians.

wiki.summary: Chichibu City's guide describes a mountain-worship shrine at about 1,100 metres; it does not authenticate the novel's theft or ambush.

novel_trigger.context: Daizō's proposed assassination assigns Matahachi an intended destination inside the castle complex.

wiki.summary: The palace grounds include the former Edo Castle complex. Narrative interiors and routes remain unmapped.

novel_trigger.context: Iori meets the Hosokawa advance party at the locality named Nobidome in the translation.

wiki.summary: Niiza City ties documented Nobidome development to 1655, later than the narrative frame; mapping is therefore blocked.

novel_trigger.context: Musashi answers the official summons at the Reception Pavilion near the gate.

wiki.summary: Official material supports Wadakura Gate as an Edo Castle remain, not the novel's Reception Pavilion or Orchid Room.
